title: The Stuff You Should Know Doin’ Science Playlist: How Occam's Razor Works
summary: A Stuff You Should Know "Doin' Science" playlist rerun of the 2018 episode on Occam's razor. The hosts explain the principle of parsimony/plurality attributed to William of Ockham, a 14th-century Franciscan monk and rationalist who clashed with the church and was excommunicated. They trace its roots to Aristotle and Robert Grosseteste, note the misattribution to Ockham (John Duns Scotus possibly the originator, per a correction), and contrast it with the medieval synthesis of Thomas Aquinas. They discuss the Lorentz vs. Einstein relativity example, positivism and Ernst Mach, and the misuse of Occam's razor by skeptics, creationists, and atheists. They argue simplicity is subjective, that it is a heuristic rather than proof, and that it doesn't settle questions like geocentric vs. heliocentric models. The episode ends with a listener mail about a North Korea "naughty Korea/nice Korea" graphic and a 2012 London Olympics dispute.

segments.title: Opening and introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces the 2018 episode on Occam's razor as a playlist rerun, and Chuck and Josh banter, including a mustache joke.

segments.title: Introducing Occam's razor
segments.summary: Hosts describe Occam's razor as the principle that the simplest explanation is probably right, and mention popular misuses such as explaining away photo orbs or the Kennedy assassination.

segments.title: Principle of plurality and parsimony
segments.summary: The two Latin-derived formulations, the principle of plurality and the principle of parsimony, are explained, and the hosts discuss how they relate. The idea is a heuristic: do not add more than needed.

segments.title: Empiricism and simplicity in science
segments.summary: Hosts link Occam's razor to empiricism, the reliance on sensory evidence, and note that simplicity is widely valued in nature and human thinking.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief break before the historical segment.

segments.title: Who was William of Ockham
segments.summary: William of Ockham is introduced as a Franciscan monk (c. 1285 to 1349) who took a vow of poverty and lived humbly.

segments.title: Origins: Aristotle, Grosseteste, and attribution
segments.summary: The idea traces back to Aristotle and is restated by Robert Grosseteste. A correction notes John Duns Scotus may have encapsulated the principle and that William Rowan Hamilton misattributed it to Ockham.

segments.title: Ockham's clash with the church
segments.summary: Ockham challenged church leaders over wealth and power, was excommunicated, sought refuge in Munich under Emperor Louis IV, and argued against Pope John XXII. The hosts contrast his views with Thomas Aquinas's medieval synthesis.

segments.title: Lorentz, Einstein, and Ernst Mach
segments.summary: The hosts compare Lorentz's ether explanation with Einstein's relativity, noting Einstein's was simpler. Positivism and Ernst Mach's rejection of molecules are discussed, and Einstein later showed molecules exist.

segments.title: Skeptics and misuse of the razor
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how true skeptics use the razor to consider alternatives, not to disprove claims. Examples include ghost photos, and the subjectivity of judging what is simplest. Scientists use it as a practical tool in machine learning, such as decision trees.

segments.title: Creationism, atheism, and simplicity in nature
segments.summary: Creationists and atheists both use the razor to argue about God, and the hosts say both misuse it. They discuss whether nature is actually simple, with examples like photosynthesis, shark fins, and cow stomachs.

segments.title: Simplicity as human construct and limits of the razor
segments.summary: The hosts argue simplicity is a human-made value and that the razor cannot settle questions like Ptolemy's geocentric model versus Copernicus's heliocentric model. Complexity is not proof of error. Art and engineering are also discussed.

segments.title: Closing discussion
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up, noting the razor can squash free thought and that it is not a rule of right or wrong.

segments.title: Article plug
segments.summary: Josh points listeners to his HowStuffWorks article on Occam's razor.

segments.title: Listener mail: North Korea and Claire Sutherland
segments.summary: Claire Sutherland, an editor at an Australian newspaper, recounts North Korea's official condemnation of her paper's 'naughty Korea, nice Korea' Olympic medal graphic during the London Olympics, and the paper's front-page coverage of it.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact info
segments.summary: Hosts give social media, email, and website contact details and sign off.
